events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Zara proposes Zara, Maya. As leader with no role information, I'm proposing myself and Maya for the 2-player Mission 1 team. Both of us are Good-aligned in my view, and this is a neutral first pick while we gather information from the discussion.

I don't have any strong reads yet this early, so I'll keep this simple. A two-player team of the leader plus Maya is a reasonable default opening, and I don't object to the leader putting themselves on Mission 1 to take responsibility for the result. What I'd like to hear is the reasoning behind the other half of the pairing. Zara, calling Maya a neutral pick is fine, but neutral for whom? On a two-player mission there is nowhere to hide — if this fails, we learn a lot, but I'd rather we not hand Evil a free look at the first mission if a better pairing exists. Maya, I'd like to hear from you directly: do you support this proposal as-is, and is there anything about your own read of the table that makes you a particularly safe pick for the leader? I'm not making any accusation here — with zero information, anyone could be anyone — but I want to hear confidence or hesitation before I decide how to vote. If both of you give me straight answers, I'm prepared to back this team.

I support the team as proposed, Isha. I know I'm Good, but I don't have a reliable read on Zara or anyone else yet, so I can't claim the pairing is proven safe. It's a reasonable opening, and the result and votes will give us something concrete to discuss.

Isha, to answer directly: by 'neutral' I meant that I had no information that would justify picking anyone else. I should correct one thing I said. I wrote that Maya and I are both Good in my view, but I only know my own alignment. I can't verify Maya's, so I'm not treating her as a confirmed Good player. Maya, thank you for answering plainly. Saying you're Good is a claim I can't check, so I'm taking your support for the team as a reason to trust the process, not as proof. I agree with Isha that a two-player mission gives Evil a look at the team. I'm open to a different pairing if someone has a concrete reason for it, and I'll weigh that before the vote. Right now my vote depends on whether the table is comfortable that this first look is worth taking.

Thank you both for answering — Zara's correction was honest and Maya's response was composed. But I have to be straight with the table: something about Maya's answer didn't sit right with me, and on a two-player mission, 'composed' is exactly what a well-prepared Evil player looks like. Maya said she supports the team and knows she's Good, but she gave us nothing beyond the bare claim — no read on anyone, no reasoning for why she specifically is the safe second pick. On a mission with no spare seats, a bare claim is the cheapest thing in the game to make. I said earlier I was prepared to back this team if I got straight answers, and I got answers, but not the kind that settle my concern. A first mission that fails hands Evil information and hands us suspicion with no way to trace it, and I'd rather not start this game by gambling a seat on someone whose only qualification is volunteering for it. Zara, I want to ask you directly: you said you're open to a different pairing if someone has a concrete reason — I'm telling you my concrete reason is that Maya's response gave us confidence without content, and that on a two-player team that pattern worries me more than any argument I've heard for keeping her. Would you consider swapping her for Elena, who hasn't had to say anything yet precisely because she hasn't volunteered herself into the spotlight? Self-selection is a real signal in this game, and right now it's pointing somewhere I don't like. I'm not calling Maya Evil — I can't prove anything this early, and she may well be exactly who she says she is. But with two seats and three other candidates, the burden should be on the player who asked to be on the team, not on the rest of us to justify our doubts. If Zara keeps the team as-is, I'll have to weigh my vote accordingly.

Isha, thank you for asking directly. I won't swap Maya for Elena on the current reasoning. Maya volunteering for a team is not evidence of anything, and Elena staying quiet is not evidence either. Neither of them has said anything yet that would justify moving a seat. I also want to be clear that I'm not claiming Maya is Good. I know only my own alignment, and I'm not treating her support as proof. Maya's answer was plain and gave us a stated position we can test. A two-player mission is risky, and I understand your concern about a bare claim. But if we replace a player because of who asked to be picked, we are using a signal that could just as easily point at Elena. My honest view is that the team should be judged on what we learn from its result and from what each member says from here on. You told the table that a concrete reason would change your thinking, and that your concern is the pattern of Maya's answer. What specific response from Maya, or what specific point from anyone, would move you to approve this team?

Zara, you asked me a direct question, so I'll give you a direct answer: there is no specific response from Maya that would settle my concern, because my concern was never about the quality of her answer. It was about the fact that a two-player team leaves no room for error, and Maya's case for inclusion rests entirely on a claim I cannot check and a self-nomination I cannot evaluate. If the standard for keeping her is that nothing concrete has been said against her, then the standard is too low for a mission this size — the standard should be something concrete in her favor, and so far there is nothing. That is not a flaw in Maya's delivery; it is a structural problem with picking the first volunteer and calling it neutral. I want to be fair to you, Zara: you corrected your own statement unprompted, you have been precise about what you know and don't know, and I have no issue with your leadership on this team. That precision is exactly why I'm puzzled that the same rigor isn't being applied to the second seat. You said moving a seat based on self-selection is a signal that could just as easily point at Elena. But Elena isn't the one asking for a seat — Maya is. The asymmetry matters: one player volunteered onto a two-person mission where a single fail card is untraceable, and the other has simply not spoken yet. Silence is not evidence of goodness, but volunteering is also not evidence of goodness, and when the two are weighed against each other on a team with no spare seat, I'd rather take the player who hasn't reached for the spotlight. So here is my position, plainly: if the team stays Zara and Maya, I will vote against it. Not as an accusation I can prove — I can't — but as a judgment call about risk on a mission where a fail would leave us with suspicion and no way to trace it. If you revise to include Elena, I will vote to approve, because that pairing gives us the same experienced leadership with a second seat whose selection tells us nothing suspicious either way. Zara, before you finalize: you have one revision available. Would you use it to replace Maya with Elena rather than stake the first mission on a pairing that at least one player has already told you they'll vote down? I'm asking because a rejected proposal costs the whole table time and hands information to whoever is watching, and I'd rather resolve this now than force a vote you may lose. Whatever you decide, I'll respect the process — but I wanted my answer on the record before the vote, not after.

Isha, thank you for stating your position plainly. I want to correct one point first: I chose Maya, Maya did not nominate herself. I proposed myself and Maya on the basis of no information, so the self-selection concern applies to my choice, not to hers. I still have no evidence that Maya is Evil, and I also have no evidence that Elena is Good, so swapping on the basis of who volunteered would just replace one unknown with another. I'm not treating Maya's support as proof, and I won't treat Elena's silence as proof either. I understand that you would vote against a team with Maya on it, and I respect that this is a judgment about risk on a two-player mission. My view is that the team should be judged on concrete information, and we have none about either candidate yet. I'll weigh any specific, checkable reason before the final decision, and I'm open to revising if someone gives one. For now I'm keeping Zara and Maya, and I'd ask the table to tell me what concrete information would change their minds.

I have no private information beyond my own alignment, so I won't pretend to have a read on Zara or Maya. Looking at the proposal itself, Zara has been consistent: she corrected her earlier wording, acknowledged she cannot vouch for Maya, and kept the team while inviting concrete reasons to change it. Isha's concern about risk on a two-player mission is reasonable, but I agree with Zara that the self-selection point does not really apply here, since Zara chose Maya rather than Maya volunteering herself onto the team. Maya's answer was not proof of anything, but it was clear and did not overclaim. With no concrete information against either player, I do not see a strong reason to reject this team solely because it is the first proposal. I also do not think silence from me should be treated as evidence either way. At this stage I am inclined to approve the proposed team unless something more specific emerges, and I will judge the mission result and the votes as the real information we gain.

I agree with the points Zara and Elena have made. Isha's primary concern seemed to be that Maya volunteered herself into the spotlight, but as Zara pointed out, Zara was the one who selected Maya in the initial proposal. Maya simply gave a standard, direct answer when asked. On the very first proposal of Mission 1, none of us have concrete reads yet, so treating a composed, straightforward response as suspicious feels like overthinking a standard opening. Zara has been transparent about her thought process, and replacing Maya with another unknown doesn't actually provide us with any better security. I don't see a solid reason to reject this proposal and burn an attempt, so I am inclined to support the team and let the mission outcome provide our first real data.

I remain inclined to approve the proposed team of Zara and Maya. Zara has been transparent about the limits of her information and kept the team while inviting concrete reasons to change it. Maya gave a direct answer without overclaiming. I take Isha's concern about a two-player mission seriously, but I do not see concrete evidence against Maya, and replacing her with another unknown would not by itself make the team safer. At this stage the mission result and the votes are the information we actually need.

Zara confirms Zara, Maya. I'm keeping Zara and Maya. Nobody has given concrete evidence against Maya, and swapping her for Elena would only replace one unknown with another. The mission result and votes will give us real information.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Isha proposes Isha, Elena, Zara. Mission 1 failed with exactly one fail card, which came from either Zara or Maya. Zara has been the most precise and self-correcting player at the table, and her conduct does not fit the profile of someone who just sank the first mission, while Maya's only contribution so far has been a bare claim of goodness followed by defending a team that failed. Omar spoke up quickly to shut down Isha's entirely reasonable risk concerns before the vote, which I also find notable. I'm putting myself on the team to take direct responsibility for the result, and choosing Elena and Zara, whose behavior so far has been consistent and measured. I understand this leaves off two players who supported the last proposal, but that proposal produced a fail, so I'm prioritizing the players whose records give me the most confidence in a clean result.

Isha, the fail could have come from either Zara or me. Zara's careful wording is not proof of her alignment, just as my support for the team is not proof against me. Omar's approval also tells us little: Elena approved that team too.

I know I didn't fail the mission, so I suspect Zara. I can't expect the rest of you to take my word for that, but keeping Zara while excluding both me and Omar assumes an answer the public result doesn't provide. Isha, would you consider replacing Zara with Omar so this team doesn't include either member of the failed mission?

Maya, I'm not replacing Zara with Omar, and I want to explain why on the record. Your proposal doesn't even follow your own stated principle. You've framed this as 'exclude both members of the failed mission,' but Omar voted to approve that exact team and then spoke first to wave away my risk concerns before the vote. If approving and defending the failed team is disqualifying, then Omar is disqualified by exactly the same standard you're applying to Zara. You cannot hold that principle and recommend Omar in the same breath.

Zara, meanwhile, has been the most transparent player at this table. She corrected her own statement unprompted before the mission even happened, she was precise about what she knew and didn't know, and she explicitly said she couldn't vouch for Maya's alignment. That is not the conduct of someone who then secretly failed the mission. It is, however, exactly the kind of honesty that makes her a useful scapegoat for whoever did fail it.

Because only one fail card was played, the fail came from Maya or Zara — full stop. So I have to weigh two candidates. One of them volunteered a bare claim of goodness, gave us no reasoning when directly pressed by Elena's question and my own, and now, the very first chance she gets, is trying to engineer a team swap that would put a different player under suspicion while deflecting from herself. The other corrected herself publicly when it cost her nothing, invited concrete reasons to change her proposal, and accepted the vote. Maya, notice also what your request would do structurally: it replaces the player you're accusing with a player you haven't accused, while leaving you — the other possible source of the fail card — off the team entirely with no consequences. That's a very comfortable outcome for you no matter what the truth is.

So my position is straightforward: I'm keeping this team as Isha, Elena, and Zara. I take responsibility for the result as leader. If Zara had any realistic motive or opening to fail that mission, I'd reconsider — but I see none, and Maya's redirect at Zara gives me no new information about anything except Maya's own instincts about where to point fingers.

Maya, I'll put one question to you directly: if excluding everyone who supported the failed team is genuinely your principle, why did you name Omar — who approved it and defended it — rather than Elena, who also approved it but whom nobody suspects? And if approving the failed team isn't disqualifying for Omar, then why is it disqualifying for Zara? I'd like a direct answer before the vote, because the internal contradiction in your request is the first concrete thing anyone has offered since the mission failed, and it points in a direction I'd like you to explain.

Isha, my principle was to exclude both players who went on the failed mission, not everyone who approved the team. Elena is already on your proposed team, so Omar is the remaining replacement for Zara. Approving a team that later fails is not the same as being one of the two people who could have played the fail card.

I understand why you trust Zara's careful statements, but an Evil player can correct their wording and acknowledge uncertainty too. The public result does not establish whether Zara or I failed. Replacing Zara with Omar would avoid putting either possible source of that fail on this mission; keeping Zara relies on your read of her behavior being right. I still urge you to make that swap.

Maya, I appreciate that you clarified your principle, but the clarification makes the problem worse, not better. Your refined position is: exclude the two mission members, keep everyone who approved the team, and slot Omar in. Let's examine what that actually means. Under your principle, you exclude yourself from the team — fine — but you also treat yourself as settled. You told the table 'I know I didn't fail the mission,' and you expect that sentence to do all the work. It can't. Only one fail card was played, so the fail came from you or Zara, and your certainty about yourself is exactly as checkable as the bare claim of goodness you offered in Mission 1 — which is to say, not checkable at all. Meanwhile, Zara's case is not merely my 'read of her behavior.' Zara corrected her own statement unprompted, told the table explicitly that she could not vouch for Maya's alignment, invited concrete reasons to change the proposal, and accepted the vote without complaint. That is a public, verifiable record of conduct. Your counter is that 'an Evil player can correct their wording too' — true, but it proves nothing except that no claim is beyond mimicry, which cuts equally against your own assertions. So the asymmetry in your argument is this: your self-assessment is treated as fact, and the only other candidate's documented conduct is treated as noise. That asymmetry is the tell I'm asking the table to weigh. And notice where your principle deposits the seat: with Omar, who rushed to dismiss my risk concerns before the last vote and who, like you, has offered no concrete evidence for anything. I am not replacing Zara with Omar. I am keeping this team — me, Elena, Zara — and I take responsibility for its result. Maya, one direct question before the vote: if your certainty that you played Success is acceptable evidence, why is Zara's documented record of transparency not at least as strong evidence for her?

Isha, my certainty about my own card is private information that I cannot prove to the table. Zara's transparency is public, but it is not a guarantee of alignment; an Evil player can be careful and self-correct too.

My suggestion to exclude both mission members does not require anyone to take my claim on faith. It avoids both possible sources of the fail. I still think Isha, Elena, Omar is the safer proposal than retaining Zara.

I'll state this plainly because I'm on the proposed team. I am Good, and I submitted Success on Mission 1. That is my own card, and I'm sharing it because the single fail came from one of the two players on that team, Maya or me. Since I know mine was Success, the only remaining source is Maya. Maya, your request to swap me for Omar asks the table to remove the one team member who can confirm her own card and put in a player who approved the failed team. That does not reduce risk. It moves the exposure to someone you have not accused. Isha, your concerns about Maya's bare claim and her immediate push to reshape the team have held up. Elena, you are on this team and approved the Mission 1 proposal, so I'd like your direct read: knowing the fail came from one of the two Mission 1 members and that I played Success, do you still see a reason to remove me from Isha's team?

Zara, to answer your direct request: no, I do not see a sufficient reason to remove you from Isha’s team. I know my own alignment, and I have no private read on either Zara or Maya. The public fact is narrow: Mission 1 failed with exactly one fail card, so it came from Zara or Maya. Zara now states she submitted Success; Maya states she submitted Success. Neither claim is independently checkable. But Maya’s response to the failure has been to push a swap that would remove Zara and seat Omar, who approved and defended the failed team. Even after Maya clarified that her principle was to exclude the two mission members, her proposal still leaves the table relying on her private certainty while treating Zara’s public conduct as noise. I agree an Evil player can be careful and self-correct, but that argument cuts both ways and gives me no reason to prefer Maya over Zara. Zara’s record—correcting her own wording, explicitly saying she could not vouch for Maya, inviting concrete reasons to change the first proposal, and accepting the vote—is at least public evidence of consistency. Maya’s certainty about her own card is not public evidence. I also do not think replacing Zara with Omar improves safety; it shifts the seat to another unknown who supported the failed team. I will vote to approve Isha, Elena, and Zara. I take Isha’s point that this is a judgment call, not proof. My judgment is that the proposed team is cleaner than the alternative Maya has pushed, and I want the next mission result to give us more data.

I need to address how my name has been brought into this. Maya suggesting me as a replacement for Zara was entirely her own idea, and her using me to deflect suspicion does not do me any favors. Furthermore, Isha's accusation that I was trying to shut down concerns on Mission 1 is unfounded. I stated that swapping an unknown for an unknown on proposal 1 without evidence did not make sense, which was the exact same reasoning Elena offered, and Elena voted to approve just as I did. Singling me out for that vote while giving Elena a pass is inconsistent. More importantly, look at the actual risk on this proposal. Mission 1 failed with one fail card. That is an indisputable fact: either Maya or Zara is Evil. That means putting Zara on this team carries an immediate 50% risk of seating an Evil player. Zara's defense is that she is polite, self-correcting, and claims she played Success. But if Zara is Evil and failed Mission 1, acting measured and claiming Success is the exact line she has to take. Politeness is not alignment. If Zara is Evil, approving this team hands Evil their second win and puts the entire game on the brink. Elena, you mentioned that taking an untested player does not improve safety, but Zara is not merely untested; she has a direct 50% chance of having sabotaged Mission 1. Why take a coin-flip gamble on a failed mission member when we have fresh players who could not have played that fail card?

Omar, I take your point seriously: Zara is not untested in the sense of having no public history, because she was on the failed Mission 1 team. But the public result does not tell us which of Zara or Maya played the fail card, and both have now stated they submitted Success. That claim is not independently checkable from either of them. What I can weigh is their conduct after the failure. Maya’s first response was to push a swap that removes Zara and seats you, while leaving herself off the team; even after she clarified her principle, her argument still depends on her private certainty about her own card and treats Zara’s public consistency as noise. Zara, by contrast, corrected her own wording before Mission 1, explicitly said she could not vouch for Maya, invited concrete reasons to change her proposal, accepted the vote, and has now made a direct claim about her own card. Neither claim proves alignment, but I do not see Maya’s redirect as making the team safer. I also do not accept that replacing Zara with you improves the table’s information: it shifts the seat to another unknown and leaves the central Zara-or-Maya question unresolved. For that reason I remain inclined to approve Isha, Elena, and Zara. I know my own alignment, but I cannot prove it to the table; I can only say that I supported this team before and I still believe it is the cleaner proposal than the alternative Maya has pushed. I will vote to approve the proposed team.

Omar, you've reframed my earlier observation as an accusation, so let me correct the record before addressing your argument. I never said your approval of the Mission 1 team was disqualifying — I noted that you spoke first to wave away risk concerns before that vote, and I noted it because Maya then chose you, of all people, as her replacement. My point was about who benefits from her redirect, not about who voted how. Your complaint that Elena got a pass misses this: Elena's reasoning was that swapping an unknown for an unknown changed nothing. Your framing now is different — you're actively campaigning to seat a player you call a 50% risk and to keep one of the two possible fail sources off every team. Those are not the same position. Now, your 50% argument. You're right that the fail card came from Zara or Maya, and that Zara carries risk. But by your own math, so does Maya — and Maya's response to the failure has been the most informative thing anyone has done since the vote. Her first move was to engineer a swap that removed Zara, seated you, and left herself untouched. Her stated principle — exclude the two mission members — required replacing Zara with someone, and she picked the player her argument had not accused. When Isha pressed her on why Omar and not Elena, her answer was procedural, not principled. That is a pattern, and it points somewhere specific. Zara's record, by contrast, is public and consistent: she corrected her own statement unprompted, she refused to claim knowledge she didn't have, she invited concrete reasons to change her proposal, and she accepted the vote. She has now claimed she played Success. I can't check that claim, but I can check the behavior around it — and nothing in Zara's conduct resembles someone managing a cover story. Maya's conduct does. So the real choice in front of the table is not 'coin-flip on Zara versus fresh players.' It's this: every version of a safe team still has to exclude exactly one of Zara or Maya, and the evidence we've generated since the fail — who redirected, who deflected, who answered direct questions with direct answers — all favors excluding Maya and keeping Zara. Your proposal does the opposite while describing itself as the cautious option. Omar, I'll ask you one direct question, and I'd like a straight answer: if seating a possible fail source is disqualifying, why did Maya's version of the safe team keep every seat available to you while the only seat she was willing to sacrifice was Zara's — the seat belonging to the one player whose documented conduct contradicts Maya's story? If you can answer that without another deflection onto me or Elena, I'll weigh it. If the answer is that Maya's principle only ever seemed to move seats away from Zara and toward you, then the table should ask what that principle was actually for. I'm keeping this

Isha, the answer to your question is simple arithmetic, not a conspiracy: in a five-player game, if a three-person team excludes both members of the failed Mission 1 (Maya and Zara), the only three players remaining at the table are you, Elena, and me. Elena was already on your draft, so if Maya's stated principle was to exclude both Mission 1 participants, there was literally no other player in the game she could have named besides me. Framing her suggestion as a calculated maneuver to favor me over other alternatives completely ignores that no other alternatives existed mathematically.

I am not campaigning to be seated, nor am I defending Maya. My point from the beginning has been about risk management. We know with mathematical certainty that either Zara or Maya submitted the fail card. By including Zara, you are taking a 50% coin flip on an active fail source. If your behavioral read of Zara's transparency and composure is mistaken, you hand Evil a 2-0 lead and put the entire game on the brink. Measured language and self-corrections are tools an Evil player can easily adopt to build trust. If you and Elena are convinced that Zara's demeanor outweighs that structural risk, you have the votes to approve the mission, but the table should be clear-eyed about the gamble being taken.

I'm on this team, so I'll be direct. I submitted Success on Mission 1, which is my own card. Good players must choose Success, so the one Fail card came from Maya. Omar, that means the 50% framing doesn't describe my position: I know my own card, and I could not have played the fail. The table can't check my card directly, so I'm not asking anyone to take it purely on faith. I'm asking you to weigh it against what happened after the fail. Maya's first move was to push a swap that removed me and seated you, while keeping herself off the team. When Isha asked why she named you rather than Elena, her answer was procedural. Her repeated line that she knows she didn't fail is the same kind of unverifiable claim she holds against me, and she has used it to justify a team that excludes her. Isha's team of Isha, Elena, and Zara includes a player whose Success card has been stated publicly and a leader who has taken responsibility for the result. I'd rather approve that than swap in a player who approved the failed team for the one whose card is now on the record. Omar, do you accept that once I have stated my card is Success, the fail must be Maya's? If not, which part of my statement do you think is false, and why?

Zara, of course I don't accept that premise, because it is entirely circular. Maya stated with equal conviction that she submitted Success. By your exact logic, if Maya says she played Success, then by definition you must have played the Fail. Both of you cannot simultaneously be proven innocent purely by your own word, which means an unverified claim from either of you proves nothing to the rest of the table. If an Evil player had failed Mission 1, their only viable public play is to claim they submitted Success and accuse the other person—which is precisely what you are doing, and precisely what Maya did. I don't have private knowledge of which one of you is Evil, but asking the table to treat your self-declaration as mathematical certainty is absurd. Do you genuinely believe that simply asserting you played Success eliminates the risk of you being the player who failed Mission 1?

Omar, to answer directly: no, my Success card does not make me immune, and I can't prove it to you. Nothing any of us says can prove our card. That is why the table should weigh conduct and the logic of each request. Mission 1 had exactly one Fail card. I know mine was Success, so the Fail came from Maya. Maya has said she also submitted Success, but she has offered no way to check that claim. Her first response to the failure was to remove me, seat you, and leave herself off the team. When she clarified her principle, it still left you as the only possible replacement, and she has not explained why that outcome matters. You have pressed the same swap several ways, and I don't think the 50% framing fits the evidence. A fail card was played by one of the two members, and I can state where mine went. The question for the table is which team is safer: Isha, Elena and me, whose leader has taken responsibility and whose members have answered direct questions, or a team built to move the failed mission's most evasive redirect out of the room. I'm not asking anyone to treat my word as mathematical certainty. I am asking the table to weigh the behavior after the fail, and that behavior points at Maya. I will vote to approve Isha, Elena and Zara.

Isha confirms Isha, Elena, Zara. I'm keeping the team of Isha, Elena, and Zara. The single fail card on Mission 1 came from Maya or Zara, and everything since then points at Maya: her first move after the fail was to engineer a swap that removed Zara, seated Omar, and left herself untouched, and her only evidence has been unverifiable claims about her own card. Omar pressed hard to seat a possible fail source while dismissing Zara's stated card, which does not reassure me either. Zara's conduct has been consistent and transparent throughout. This lineup excludes both players whose behavior concerns me, and I take responsibility for the result as leader.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Maya proposes Zara, Omar. Mission 2 succeeded with Zara aboard, and Omar’s concerns about the earlier proposal were reasonable. I propose testing that pairing.

Let me put the record in order before we vote, because Mission 2's result actually settles more than people are giving it credit for. Mission 2 succeeded with zero fail cards, and it included Zara. Combined with Mission 1 — one fail card, from Zara or Maya — we now have a player who was on a failed mission, was accused, then went onto a three-person team and delivered a clean result. That does not prove Zara is Good, but it is real, concrete information, and it makes Maya — who has been the one pressing unverifiable claims about her own card while engineering swaps that always benefited herself — the remaining suspect for the Mission 1 fail. Zara is, on the public record, the least suspicious player at this table right now.

Which brings me to Omar. I want to walk through his Mission 2 conduct, because it was striking. He approved the Mission 1 team that failed. When I raised entirely ordinary risk concerns about a two-player mission, he was the one who jumped in first to wave them off. Then, the moment that mission failed, he campaigned hard to characterize Zara as a 50% coin-flip on an active fail source, demanded she be kept off teams, and dismissed her stated card as worthless — while endorsing a swap that would have seated himself. Now, the player I consider the most likely source of that fail card, Maya, proposes a team pairing Omar with that same Zara he spent an entire discussion calling a dangerous gamble. If Omar genuinely believed his own Mission 2 argument, seating Zara now should alarm him. If he no longer believes it, then his entire Mission 2 campaign against her was noise, and I'd like to know what changed.

Omar, directly: you spent Mission 2 insisting Zara might be the fail source and that her claimed Success proved nothing. Mission 2 has since succeeded with her aboard, which is exactly the kind of evidence you said the table needed. Do you now accept that your campaign against Zara was misplaced — and if you do, why should we trust the judgment of a player who argued that forcefully from a position that the very next result contradicted? And if you still suspect her, why are you accepting a two-player seat beside her?

Isha, to answer you directly: first, I have not 'accepted' this seat. Maya drafted this team without consulting me, just as she threw my name into Mission 2 discussion without my involvement. You are framing this as though I lobbied for the spot or accepted it, when in reality Maya is the leader making the pick.

Second, regarding my Mission 2 stance: advocating caution when facing a 50% risk on an unconfirmed fail source was sound risk management based on the information we had. That Mission 2 succeeded is great for Good, but pointing out structural risk before the cards are played is not an error in judgment—it's prudence. Furthermore, an Evil player on a three-person mission has clear strategic incentives to submit Success to secure trust for the rest of the game. That said, the more straightforward conclusion from Mission 2 succeeding is that Maya is overwhelmingly likely the player who failed Mission 1.

Which leads directly to why we should be cautious of this proposal. If Maya is the Evil player from Mission 1—which the board now strongly suggests—we must evaluate why she is proposing Zara and me. She knows she cannot seat herself, so she pairs Zara (who currently holds the table's trust) with me, likely trying to exploit the debate from Mission 2 to create confusion or force another split vote.

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
